title: Use radix sorting for order() in as_list()
description:
The test suite broke as we tried updating 1.1.0 -> 1.2.0:

```
── Failure (test-map.R:247:3): Sorting keys ────────────────────────────────────
m$as_list(sort = TRUE) not identical to list(.d = 4, a = 1, b = 2, c = 3).
Names: 4 string mismatches
Component 1: Mean relative difference: 3
Component 2: Mean relative difference: 0.5
Component 3: Mean relative difference: 0.3333333
Component 4: Mean relative difference: 0.25
```

I'm not sure why this isn't showing up on CRAN or on your end. 

But I do see `method="radix"` under `sort` explicitly elsewhere, and this does make tests pass for me, so I think this is a good change regardless.

title: Add functional methods for fastmap
description:
Closes #25.

This adds the following methods to `fastmap`:

* `map()`, `map_with_key()`
* `filter()`, `filter_with_key()`, `filter_key()`
* `modify()`, `modify_with_key()`: like `map` methods, but modifies in place.
* `walk()`, `walk_with_key()`: like `map` methods, but doesn't collect return values.

I'd also like to add methods to filter in place, but need a good name for it.

title: Fix `unserialize(serialize())` behavior when there are no holes
Add `clone()` method
description:
Closes #24.

This is significantly faster than manual copying. For a million objects, it's about 0.14 seconds vs 3 seconds on my computer.


```R
library(fastmap)

rm(list=ls())
n <- 1e6
x <- seq_len(n)

m <- fastmap()
m$mset(.list = setNames(x, as.character(x)))


# stla's copy function
invisible(gc())
copy <- function(map) {
  fm <- fastmap()
  for(k in map$keys()) {
    fm$set(k, map$get(k))
  }
  fm
}
system.time({
  m2 <- copy(m)
})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   2.992   0.030   3.025


# clone() method
invisible(gc())
system.time({
  m4 <- m$clone()
})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.008   0.005   0.014
```

title: Switch from std::unordered_map to tsl::hopscotch_map
description: Closes #8. `tsl::hopscotch_map` should be faster than `std::unordered_map`, and also have stable behavior across platforms. The order of keys is still not guaranteed to be consistent across platforms -- platforms that don't support C++11 will have a `std::map`, which, unlike `tsl::hopscotch_map`, sorts the keys -- but in practice any platform that has a C++11 compiler will use `tsl::hopscotch_map` and therefore have a consistent ordering, which will reduce the likelihood of encountering hard-to-diagnose cross-platform bugs.

title: Convert map to use const char* instead of std::string
description:
This PR is mostly for future reference. It changes the map data structure from `std::unordered_map<std::string, int>` to `std::unordered_map<const char*, int>`, as suggested by @jimhester.

Speed and memory usage appear to be essentially same. When running this code, I get the same output for both master and this branch:

```R
{
  library(fastmap)
  library(pryr)
  gc()
  start_mem <- mem_used()
  start_time <- as.numeric(Sys.time())
  cat("start mem: ")
  print(start_mem)
  for (i in 1:8) {
    m <- fastmap()
    for (j in 1:50000) {
      x <- as.character(runif(1))
      m$set(x, x)
    }
    cat(i, ": ", sep = "")
    print(mem_used())
    rm(m, x)
  }
  end_time <- as.numeric(Sys.time())
  gc()
  end_mem <- mem_used()
  cat("end mem: ")
  print(end_mem)
  cat("Elapsed time:", round(end_time - start_time, 1), "seconds\n")
  cat("Memory leaked:", end_mem - start_mem, "bytes\n")
}
```


The result of the third run after starting R, with master:

```
start mem: 42.5 MB
1: 63.4 MB
2: 63.4 MB
3: 63.4 MB
4: 63.4 MB
5: 63.4 MB
6: 63.4 MB
7: 63.4 MB
8: 63.4 MB
end mem: 42.5 MB
Elapsed time: 5.6 seconds
Memory leaked: 0 bytes
```

With this PR:

```
start mem: 42.5 MB
1: 63.4 MB
2: 63.4 MB
3: 63.4 MB
4: 63.4 MB
5: 63.4 MB
6: 63.4 MB
7: 63.4 MB
8: 63.4 MB
end mem: 42.5 MB
Elapsed time: 5.4 seconds
Memory leaked: 0 bytes
```

The `const char*` version is ever so slightly faster. Surprisingly, it does not use any less memory than the `std::string` version, at least not enough to show up in this test.

The drawback to the `const char*` version is it points to objects in R's string pool, and it requires something else to prevent those objects from being garbage collected. The [`keys_`](https://github.com/r-lib/fastmap/blob/fe3492285c3eba35edd48a7484d8433b658ebd62/R/fastmap.R#L159) object in R does this, by keeping a reference to the `CHARSXP`s, but this setup adds complexity and risk of problems in the future.
